title: Group 6 - Acute coronary syndrome and Africa
text:
Who arrives in acute coronary crisis, which habits travel with that crisis, and where in Africa is life short?

This sentence stays at the top. Every panel must attach to it. If a plot cannot be introduced in a clause that hangs off this line, it is off the wall.

section: Hunch 1 — Friends vs House vs Modern Family
text:
Hunch 1 — Friends vs House vs Modern Family

Prepare the data

hunch_1 <- hunch_1 |>
  janitor::clean_names()

names(hunch_1)

[1] "students"      "friends"       "house"         "modern_family"


The ratings are stored as text such as 7/10. Convert them to numbers, then put the three shows into one column so their ratings can be compared.

hunch_1_mod <- hunch_1 |>
  mutate(
    friends = readr::parse_number(friends),
    house = readr::parse_number(house),
    modern_family = readr::parse_number(modern_family)
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(friends, house, modern_family),
    names_to = "show",
    values_to = "scores"
  )

A case is one student who was asked to rate the TV shows. The students column is an identifier for each respondent. The ratings for Friends, House, and Modern Family are quantitative variables because the students rated the shows out of 10. Missing values mean a respondent did not provide a rating for that show.


2. Ask
Q1. How do the ratings differ between Friends, House, and Modern Family when each pair of shows is compared?


3. Choose a mark
I will use a bar chart to compare the average ratings of the three TV shows. The x-axis will represent the shows, and the y-axis will represent their average ratings. An ANOVA test will help determine whether the mean ratings differ statistically.


4. Predict
I predict that the average ratings will differ between the three shows, with one show receiving a higher average rating than the others.


5. Make

hunch_1_mean |>
  gf_col(
    mean_score ~ show,
    fill = ~ show
  ) |>
  gf_refine(
    scale_fill_manual(
      values = c(
        "friends" = "yellow",
        "house" = "lightblue",
        "modern_family" = "pink"
      )
    )
  ) |>
  gf_labs(
    title = "Which TV Show Received the Highest Rating?",
    subtitle = "Average ratings of Friends, House, and Modern Family",
    x = "TV Show",
    y = "Average Rating (out of 10)",
    fill = "TV Show",
    caption = "Source: FOSEDA Panel E, Hunch 1 dataset"
  ) |>
  gf_theme(theme_minimal(base_size = 13))










6. Say
The bar chart compares the average ratings of the three shows.
Finding to report: The show with the highest average rating is , while the show with the lowest average rating is . The ANOVA result indicates whether the differences between the mean ratings are statistically significant. Fill in these blanks after checking the graph and ANOVA output.


7. Limit
The ratings represent only the respondents in this dataset. They cannot establish which show is most popular among the general population. Missing ratings may affect the comparison because some respondents may not have watched every show. The data also cannot explain why respondents prefer one show over another.

A case is one respondent. sno is an identifier. department, mbti-type, and social-orientation are categorical variables. Check the table for missing values before interpreting the graph.


2. Ask
Q1. How are personality types distributed among SMI and MIT students, and what patterns can we find?


3. Choose a mark
I will use horizontal bar charts separated into SMI and MIT panels to compare the distribution of MBTI personality types. The bars will represent the number of students, and the panels will separate the two departments.


4. Predict
I predict that some personality types will appear more frequently than others and that the distribution may differ between SMI and MIT students.


5. Make

hunch_2 |>
  gf_bar(
    ~ `mbti-type`,
    fill = ~ `mbti-type`
  ) |>
  gf_facet_wrap(~ department) |>
  gf_labs(
    title = "Personality Types Among SMI and MIT Students",
    subtitle = "Comparing MBTI personality types across departments",
    x = "Number of Students",
    y = "MBTI Personality Type",
    fill = "MBTI Personality Type",
    caption = "Source: FOSEDA Panel E, Hunch 2 dataset (n = 60)"
  ) |>
  gf_refine(coord_flip()) |>
  gf_theme(theme_minimal(base_size = 12))










6. Say
The graph shows how frequently different MBTI personality types appear in the two departments.
Finding to report: The most frequently represented personality type in SMI is , while the most frequently represented type in MIT is . The distributions appear ___ between the two departments. Fill in the blanks after checking the graph.


7. Limit
The dataset only represents the respondents who participated in the survey. It cannot establish that studying in a particular department causes someone to have a specific personality type. The results may not represent all students at SMI or MIT.

A case is one respondent. respondent is an identifier, gender is categorical, and allowance is quantitative. Check the table for missing values and unusually high or low values.


2. Ask
Q1. Do male and female respondents receive different allowances?


3. Choose a mark
I will use a box plot with individual data points to compare allowance amounts between male and female respondents. The box plots will show the distributions, while the points will show individual responses. This will make it easier to identify differences and unusually high or low values.


4. Predict
I predict that allowance amounts will vary among respondents and that the distribution may differ between male and female students. Some students may receive considerably higher allowances than others.


5. Make

hunch_3 |>
  gf_boxplot(
    allowance ~ gender,
    fill = ~ gender,
    alpha = 0.4,
    width = 0.5
  ) |>
  gf_jitter(
    allowance ~ gender,
    color = "black",
    width = 0.12,
    height = 0,
    size = 2.5,
    alpha = 0.8
  ) |>
  gf_labs(
    title = "Do Male and Female Students Receive Different Allowances?",
    subtitle = "Comparing allowance distributions and individual responses",
    x = "Gender",
    y = "Allowance Amount",
    fill = "Gender",
    caption = "Source: FOSEDA Panel E, Hunch 3 dataset"
  ) |>
  gf_theme(theme_minimal(base_size = 13))










6. Say
The box plot compares the distribution of allowance amounts between male and female respondents. The individual points show the variation in responses and help identify unusually high values.
Finding to report: The median allowance for male respondents is , compared with for female respondents. The distributions show ___ between the two groups. Fill in the blanks after checking the graph.


7. Limit
The data cannot explain why students receive different allowance amounts or establish that gender causes these differences. An unusually high value can stretch the vertical axis and make most other observations appear close together. The findings may not represent students outside this survey.

A case is one respondent. count is an identifier, while gender, program, and AI_belief are categorical variables. The program names and response labels may have inconsistent capitalization or extra spaces, so check their values before interpreting the graph.


2. Ask
Q1. Does the relationship between gender and AI belief differ by program?


3. Choose a mark
I will use grouped bar charts separated into Art and Design panels. The x-axis will represent gender, the y-axis will show the number of respondents, and the bar colors will represent whether respondents believe in AI. This will allow me to compare responses across gender and program.


4. Predict
I predict that belief in AI may differ between male and female respondents and that this pattern may also vary between Art and Design students.


5. Make

hunch_4_clean <- hunch_4 |>
  mutate(
    gender = stringr::str_to_title(stringr::str_trim(gender)),
    program = stringr::str_to_title(stringr::str_trim(program)),
    AI_belief = stringr::str_to_title(stringr::str_trim(AI_belief))
  )

hunch_4_clean |>
  gf_bar(
    ~ gender,
    fill = ~ AI_belief,
    position = "dodge"
  ) |>
  gf_facet_wrap(~ program) |>
  gf_labs(
    title = "How Does AI Belief Vary by Gender and Program?",
    subtitle = "Comparing responses from art and design students",
    x = "Gender",
    y = "Number of Respondents",
    fill = "Belief in AI",
    caption = "Source: FOSEDA Panel E, Hunch 4 dataset"
  ) |>
  gf_theme(theme_minimal(base_size = 13))










6. Say
The graph compares Yes and No responses across genders in the Art and Design programs.
Finding to report: The distribution of AI belief appears ___ between male and female respondents in Art, while the pattern in Design appears . This suggests that the relationship between gender and AI belief across the two programs. Fill in the blanks after checking the graph.


7. Limit
The data records the respondents’ beliefs but does not explain why those beliefs exist. It cannot establish that gender or academic program causes a particular belief. The findings may not represent all art and design students.

I predict that the distribution of relationship-status responses may differ between SMI and MIT students.

The graph compares the number of respondents reporting Yes or No for relationship status across the two departments.

7. Limit
The dataset records relationship status, not how easy students find it to make friends. It cannot explain why students are or are not in relationships, measure the quality of their friendships, or establish that attending a particular institution causes differences in relationship status.

A case is one respondent. Respondents is an identifier, while Gender, Has_tattoos?, and Opinion are categorical variables. Opinion records whether the respondent thinks tattoos make people look attractive.


2. Ask
Q1. How does having tattoos relate to people’s opinions about tattoo attractiveness, and how do these opinions differ by gender?


3. Choose a mark
I will use bar charts separated by gender to compare Yes and No opinions about tattoo attractiveness. The x-axis will represent the opinions, and the y-axis will show the number of respondents.
For the simplified graph, the bar colors will represent the opinions rather than tattoo ownership. This makes the comparison between Yes and No responses within each gender easier to read. Because this graph does not use Has_tattoos?, it only answers the part of the question about opinions by gender.


4. Predict
I predict that most respondents may consider tattoos attractive, but opinions may differ between male and female respondents.


5. Make

hunch_6 |>
  mutate(
    Opinion = stringr::str_to_title(stringr::str_trim(Opinion)),
    Gender = stringr::str_to_title(stringr::str_trim(Gender))
  ) |>
  gf_bar(
    ~ Opinion,
    fill = ~ Opinion
  ) |>
  gf_facet_wrap(~ Gender) |>
  gf_labs(
    title = "Do Tattoos Make People Look Attractive?",
    subtitle = "Comparing opinions between female and male respondents",
    x = "Opinion on Tattoo Attractiveness",
    y = "Number of Respondents",
    fill = "Opinion",
    caption = "Source: FOSEDA Panel E, Hunch 6 dataset"
  ) |>
  gf_theme(theme_minimal(base_size = 13))










6. Say
The graph shows the number of male and female respondents who answered Yes or No to the question of whether tattoos make people look attractive.
Finding to report: Among female respondents, ___ answered Yes and ___ answered No. Among male respondents, ___ answered Yes and ___ answered No. This suggests that opinions about tattoo attractiveness ___ between the two groups. Fill in the blanks after checking the graph.


7. Limit
The data records opinions about tattoo attractiveness, not objective attractiveness. It cannot establish whether tattoos actually make someone more attractive or explain why respondents hold particular opinions. The simplified graph also does not show whether respondents have tattoos themselves, so it cannot establish whether tattoo ownership is related to those opinions.


8. Conclusion
